title: 3 Ways to Boost MoE Inference on NVIDIA DGX Spark | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA shows three stacked optimizations for Inclusion AI's 124B-parameter Ling-3.0-flash MoE model at batch size 1 on DGX Spark, where decoding is memory-bound: Humming MXFP4 MoE kernels, online FP8 LM-head quantization and NEXTN multi-token prediction speculative decoding. A flattering synthetic test showed +185%, but the real GSM8K result was +42.5% decode throughput and -24.5% mean latency with no accuracy loss. A silent integration bug can make the combined setup slower than the baseline.

insights.claim: At batch size 1 on NVIDIA DGX Spark, decoding Ling-3.0-flash is memory-bound: reading model weights drives execution time. The MoE expert computation and the output-layer (LM head) projection are the two dominant costs.
insights.speaker: Yang Liu
insights.so_what: On local AI boxes, memory bandwidth rather than FLOPs limits single-user inference, which favours low-bit formats and hardware with more bandwidth.
insights.quote: decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time
insights.locator: Generating tokens faster starts with identifying

insights.claim: Ling-3.0-flash is a mixture-of-experts model with 124 billion total parameters and 5.1 billion active per token. It has 42 layers, 35 Kimi Delta Attention linear-attention layers and seven MLA layers, and routes each token to 8 of 512 experts plus a shared expert. Its context window is natively 256K tokens and expandable to 1M.
insights.speaker: Yang Liu
insights.so_what: Shows Chinese open models adopting very sparse MoE and hybrid linear-attention designs for agentic long-context work, and NVIDIA actively optimizing for them.

insights.claim: The Ling-3.0-flash LM head is a 157,184 x 2,560 vocabulary GEMM stored in BF16, and its entire weight block must be read for every generated token. That makes it a high-value target for compression when bandwidth is the bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Yang Liu
insights.so_what: Large vocabularies make the output layer an often-missed bandwidth cost in edge inference.

insights.claim: Replacing the FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE backend with the independent Humming kernel library cut time per output token on DGX Spark from 27.71 ms to 25.35 ms, a 9.3% throughput gain. Humming uses NVRTC to compile kernels at runtime for the model's exact shapes, such as its narrow 768 MoE intermediate size.
insights.speaker: Yang Liu
insights.so_what: Third-party, shape-specialized kernels beat NVIDIA's own default path, a sign that the inference software stack is still fragmented and has untapped performance.

insights.claim: Humming compiles an individual kernel in seconds, whereas the FlashInfer CUTLASS path uses ninja to compile 97 targets and takes on the order of tens of minutes.
insights.speaker: Yang Liu
insights.so_what: Just-in-time kernel compilation lowers the developer-friction cost of supporting new model architectures quickly.
insights.locator: Unlike the FlashInfer CUTLASS path, Humming

insights.claim: Quantizing only the LM head online from BF16 to FP8 halves its weight reads. Combined with Humming, it lifted decode throughput 21.7% over the baseline, to 43.94 tokens per second. It is enabled with SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_LM_HEAD=1.
insights.speaker: Yang Liu
insights.so_what: Cheap, targeted precision cuts yield double-digit gains on bandwidth-bound hardware, which helps the economics of local inference.
insights.locator: The optimization applies a dynamic FP8

insights.claim: Ling-3.0-flash's built-in NEXTN layer works as a draft model with no extra training. In a synthetic test it reached 3.90 accepted tokens per round, raising throughput 185.1% over baseline to 102.88 tokens per second.
insights.speaker: Yang Liu
insights.so_what: Models that ship with native MTP heads get large 'free' speedups, which makes MTP a de facto design requirement for models meant to run on local hardware.

insights.claim: For MoE models, speculative decoding verification costs about 2.26x a normal decode step. The cost comes from expert activation rather than attention: verifying four tokens can activate up to 32 experts versus eight for one token.
insights.speaker: Yang Liu
insights.so_what: Sparse MoE models get less out of speculative decoding than dense models do, a structural tradeoff to weigh when picking architectures for local inference.
insights.quote: the cost came from MoE expert activation: a normal decode activates eight experts for one token, while verification processes four tokens and can activate up to 32 experts
insights.locator: The benefit depends on two quantities

insights.claim: Synthetic workloads systematically overestimate speculative decoding gains because of repetitive outputs, greedy sampling and fixed 2K-token outputs. Accept length fell from 3.90 on the synthetic workload to 2.68 on GSM8K, and the throughput gain fell from 185.1% to 42.5%.
insights.speaker: Yang Liu
insights.so_what: Vendor speculative-decoding speedup claims based on synthetic benchmarks should be discounted heavily, here by roughly 4x.
insights.quote: their repetitive outputs and simple sampling systematically overestimate speculative-decoding benefits

insights.claim: Across all 1,319 GSM8K questions, the three optimizations together raised decode throughput 42.5% (37.81 to 53.89 tok/s) and cut mean latency 24.5% (15.21 to 11.49 s). Accuracy was essentially unchanged at 96.82% versus 96.89%.
insights.speaker: Yang Liu
insights.so_what: Software alone delivers roughly 1.4x more usable throughput on the same DGX Spark hardware, which improves the value of local AI workstations.

insights.claim: When FP8 LM-head quantization and MTP are combined without the draft model sharing the full LM-head module, the framework silently falls back. The draft reads FP8 weights as BF16, accept length drops to 1.00, and throughput ends up lower than the unoptimized baseline.
insights.speaker: Yang Liu
insights.so_what: Stacked inference optimizations can fail silently, a deployment-reliability risk that argues for vendor-validated recipes and observability tooling.
insights.quote: the system silently degrades to a configuration slower than the unoptimized baseline

insights.claim: The optimizations combine because their mechanisms do not overlap. Humming and the FP8 LM head reduce the cost of each decode step, while MTP reduces the number of steps.
insights.speaker: Yang Liu
insights.so_what: A useful way to judge inference-stack claims is to ask whether they cut cost per step or the number of steps. Gains of the same kind usually do not stack.
